extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students (readers analyzing patent infringement issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and criteria for determining whether a given act, device, or process infringes a U.S. patent (machines, manufactures, and processes), based on case-law principles such as identity of steps, mode of operation, omission/addition of elements, and the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process patent: all claimed acts required or equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: No process patent is infringed where any one of the series of acts which constitute the process is omitted by the supposed infringer, unless some equivalent act is substituted for the one omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precisely what constitutes equivalency between acts is not rigidly defined by the Supreme Court; reasoning indicates an act is equivalent when it works in substantially the same way to accomplish the same result. Example: tamping oil wells with benzine held equivalent to tamping with water (Roberts torpedo patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition to a patented process does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An addition to a patented process does not avert infringement, even where the addition is an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the infringer adds steps or improves the process, infringement can still be found so long as the claimed steps (or equivalents) are performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order/reversal/timing of process steps generally irrelevant if same result by substantially same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the steps in the process, or not taking two or more steps simultaneously, does not avert infringement when the same result is accomplished in substantially the same way and simultaneous action is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether timing matters depends on necessity to the result or to the invention; mere chronological differences that do not change mode of operation typically do not avoid liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of a process: mere purchase does not infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: A process patent is not infringed by the purchase in the open market of a product of the process made by an infringing user of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The liability lies with the maker/user of the process; downstream purchasers (absent other acts) do not infringe the process patent merely by buying the product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines and manufactures: making/using/selling without license infringes
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a machine or manufacture is infringed by him who, without ownership or license, makes, or uses, or sells any specimen of the thing covered by any claim of that patent. Merely making without selling is an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule treats machines and manufactures together; examples and cases cited illustrate liability for unauthorized making, use, or sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only what is claimed is covered by patent; unclaimed described matter not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an infringement of a patent to make, use, or sell any specimen of any invention described but not claimed therein, because a patent covers only what it claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between descriptive disclosure and the scope defined by the claims; infringement analysis focuses on claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of any one claim infringes the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever infringes any one claim of a patent infringes the patent, whether or not the patent contains other claims which he does not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim is independently enforceable; a finding of infringement as to one claim supports a patent infringement verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results alone are not determinative; means/mode of operation matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The respective results of a patented thing and an alleged infringing thing do not furnish a criterion for infringement; identical results can be produced by substantially different means and not infringe, and different results may still be infringement if the thing is within the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on whether the accused device uses substantially the same means/mode of operation as the claimed invention, not merely whether the outcome is the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of operation as initial criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Mode of operation is a criterion of infringement: if the mode of operation of an alleged infringing thing is substantially different from that covered by the claim, infringement is negatived; if substantially the same, further tests are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mode-of-operation identity is the first of several successive tests—if the case fails on any test, infringement is not established. The nature of 'identity' is fact-dependent and usually resolved by analogy to precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode-of-operation identity is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when mode of operation is substantially the same, the charge of infringement is not necessarily affirmed; additional successive tests must be applied before concluding infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise recommends applying several successive tests (starting with mode identity) and provides multiple illustrative cases (Cawood, driven-well, Blanchard, Hayden, etc.) to guide the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition to a patented machine/manufacture does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition to a patented machine or manufacture (including duplicating parts) does not enable the maker/user/seller of the patented thing with the addition to avoid a charge of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds even where the added device facilitates operation or improves performance. However, restoring an omitted part of an older structure (when the patent claims a combination that omits that part) may not infringe the later combination if the result is a substantially different combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing relative positions of parts: function determines effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the relative positions of the parts of a machine or manufacture does not avert infringement where the parts transposed perform the same respective functions after the change as before; but if changing positions changes functions so the machine acquires a substantially different mode of operation, infringement is averted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether repositioning avoids infringement depends on whether the parts still perform the same functions in substantially the same way; cases cited (beater shaft, vapor flue) illustrate both outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element of a combination averts infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of one element or ingredient of a combination covered by any claim averts any charge of infringement based on that claim, whether or not the omitted ingredient was essential to the combination or necessary to operativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination is an entirety; if one element is omitted the claimed thing disappears. Every part of a claimed combination is conclusively presumed material; evidence to the contrary is generally inadmissible. Examples and many cases are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims to results: infringement by sufficient described devices
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee may claim so much of the described mechanism as produces a particular described result; such a claim is infringed by anyone who makes, uses, or sells an apparatus made up of enough of the described devices to produce the specified result by the specified mode of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from broad combination claims; focus on the claimed result and specified mode of operation when assessing infringement of such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniting or splitting parts does not avoid infringement if function unchanged
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniting two elements into one integral part, or separating an integral part into two, does not avoid infringement if the united or separated part performs the same function in substantially the same way as before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to functional equivalence of the structural change rather than formal arrangement; cases (Bundy, Nathan, etc.) illustrate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents: substituting an equivalent does not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No substitution of an equivalent for any ingredient of a combination covered by any claim of a patent can avert a charge of infringement of that claim, whether or not the equivalent is mentioned in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine of equivalents allows patentees to assert infringement when an accused device performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result. Conversely, substitution of something that is not an equivalent may avoid infringement. Numerous cases illustrate application of this doctrine.
